notes:
I've written up notes on Song of Solomon 1, verse by verse, from the pages I read. Most of the material comes from Guzik (Enduring Word), Ellicott, Pulpit, Gill, Spurgeon and a few evangelical sites.

**What's missing:** I didn't find anything from Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran (apart from Luther as quoted by Guzik), Pentecostal denominational, Catholic, Orthodox, NET Bible or Bible Odyssey sources, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching. Guzik's page cut off after v. 2, and Gill's after v. 4, so I only have their later verses from short extracts and summaries.

---

## The main split: allegory or love poem? (shapes the whole chapter)

- **Literal first, with a spiritual application second (Guzik).** Guzik says the best reading is a literal description of romantic and sexual love between a man and a woman. Because God uses marriage as a picture of his relationship with his people, the song also shows the love that should exist between God and the believer. He calls this a valid but *secondary* meaning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- **Luther, as quoted by Guzik.** Luther warned that allegory is uncertain and unsafe for supporting faith. Yet even Luther found a fully literal reading hard: he saw the bride as a happy, peaceful Israel under Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- **The Baptist sites disagree with each other.**
  - Spurgeon read the Song mainly as a picture of the love between Christ and his people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/ He called it the "holy of holies" of Scripture. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-bundle-of-myrrh
  - Grace to You (MacArthur) says Spurgeon and most of the Puritans confused the Song's message by allegorizing it so fully that its *primary* meaning disappeared. It reads the book as a love poem between Solomon and his bride. https://www.gty.org/articles/A398/the-rape-of-solomons-song-part-3
  - Desiring God (Piper) takes a middle path. Both the poem's sex and real sex are a kind of "life allegory": God gave us sex to show us something of his love. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-song-of-solomon-an-allegory
- **Fully allegorical (Gill).** Gill says the whole book is figurative, describing the love, union and communion between Christ and his church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm
- **Against allegory (GotQuestions).** It says the church did not exist when the Song was written, and the book can be read just as written, as a love poem. https://www.gotquestions.org/Song-of-Solomon-allegory.html
- **Precept Austin's compilers** reject both the allegorical and the "typological" approaches. The typological view treats Solomon as a real person who pictures Christ. The page says nothing in the Song shows that Solomon's life was meant to picture Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary
- **History of the debate.** Jewish tradition read the Song as God's love for Israel and Christian tradition as Christ's love for the church. Precept Austin says modern scholarship has generally rejected the allegorical approach. https://www.preceptaustin.org/song_of_solomon_commentary
- **Ellicott (older critical scholarship).** The book never mentions religion. Reading it as allegory began with the Talmud, and modern critics see a moral purpose instead of a hidden sacred meaning. In Ellicott's day the common view was that a poet from the northern kingdom wrote it, around the middle of the 10th century BC. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- Guzik says Solomon wrote it and that it was the greatest of his 1,005 songs (1 Kings 4:32). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- Ellicott says the Hebrew form means "*the* song of songs," the finest of all songs, not just "one of Solomon's songs." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Gill offers "concerning Solomon," meaning Christ, whom Solomon foreshadowed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm
- The Gospel Coalition course also reads the title as "the best of songs." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/course/song-of-solomon/

**v. 2**
- **Literal:** Guzik hears the maiden's passionate longing. He sees a strong woman who speaks most of the book, while the man still leads: she asks *him* to kiss her and to draw her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- Pulpit says the verse expresses delight that the royal bridegroom is coming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Ellicott says "love" is plural in Hebrew, meaning caresses. He notes another reading, "let him give me to drink." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- **Allegorical:** For Gill the kisses are fresh signs of Christ's love, given through his promises. Christ's love beats wine because it is pure, plentiful and free. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm
- Spurgeon preached a whole sermon on Christ's love being better than wine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/song-of-solomon-1.html
- Fausset's dictionary reads the verse as the church longing for Christ's first coming. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/fbd/s/solomon.html

**v. 3**
- Ellicott says the general sense is plain, but the grammar makes an exact translation uncertain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Gill: the ointments are Christ's grace. The name is especially "Messiah" (anointed one). The maidens are faithful churches or believers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott says the "dramatic" theory of the book rests largely on this verse. He reads it instead as the vow of love from vv. 2–3 said again in another form. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Pulpit takes the whole verse as the bride speaking. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/1-4.htm
- The NIV gives "We rejoice…" to the "Friends." https://www.blueletterbible.org/niv/sng/1/1/s_672001
- **Allegorical:** Gill says "draw me" is not about first conversion but about being brought nearer to Christ. Nobody runs after him without first being drawn. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm
- Spurgeon says the plural "loves" shows the different ways Christ's love is expressed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/song-of-solomon-1.html
- The Pulpit Homiletics compares God bringing sinners into his inner rooms to a "miracle of love." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/songs/1.htm

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: "black" means sunburnt, not that she was Pharaoh's daughter. It points to a country girl from the north. It rejects allegorical readings of this verse as forcing the text. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Ellicott calls it playful teasing that ends in a compliment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Barnes says Kedar's tents were black goat-hair. He also reports that the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase) saw Israel in the wilderness here, and some Christians saw the newly converted Gentile church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/songs/1-5.htm
- A devotional reading: black in ourselves, lovely in Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/song-of-solomon/1-5.html

**v. 6**
- Ellicott and Pulpit agree:
  - "Mother's sons" means her brothers.
  - The neglected "vineyard" is her complexion, not her virginity.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Guzik reports Trapp's guesses that "the sun" means Christ or original sin. He uses them to show the weakness of mainly allegorical reading. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/song-of-solomon/song-of-solomon-1.cfm
- Spurgeon applies the verse to Christian workers who care for others but neglect their own souls. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/and-we-are-a-jewel-from-the-revised-version/

**v. 7**
- Guzik says the shepherd image is probably symbolic, since a king was seen as a shepherd to his people. Some readers use it to argue for a separate shepherd lover, but Guzik thinks it is Solomon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- Ellicott says "veiled" follows the Greek translation and its meaning is hard to pin down. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Pulpit says the bride's main thought is being set apart for her husband. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Spurgeon preached this verse as the church's sure love for Christ. https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/sermons11/sermons11.xxix.html

**v. 8**
- Pulpit gives the verse to a chorus of ladies. It is a gentle reply, not irony. https://biblehub.com/songs/1-8.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Ellicott notes that dramatic-theory readers take it as mockery of her low birth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew means "mare." Pharaoh's horses were famous for quality, and kings of Israel bought them at high prices (1 Kings 10:29). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Pulpit: the king speaks, praising her stately grace. Older commentators saw God's love at the Exodus here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Guzik says the image probably has a sexual sense, like a mare loose among stallions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/song-of-solomon-1/
- Fausset (allegorical) sees the Red Sea deliverance. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/fbd/s/solomon.html

**vv. 10–11**
- Ellicott: dramatic readers make v. 11 a seductive offer from Solomon to the country girl. Ellicott says it is simply a loving man wanting to adorn her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- Gill reads it as Christ promising more grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm

**vv. 12–14**
- Pulpit: these are the bride's words of delight in the king. The banquet is a familiar picture of shared love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Spurgeon's sermon "A Bundle of Myrrh" is on v. 13. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/a-bundle-of-myrrh
- Gill: she shows how precious Christ is to her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm

**v. 15**
- Pulpit: the dove stands for love. The king sees purity, faithfulness and affection in her eyes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Gill: Christ notices her modest look. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm

**vv. 16–17**
- Pulpit: the bride is speaking, which the Hebrew grammar (a masculine "you") confirms. It calls v. 17 abrupt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/songs/1.htm
- Ellicott: the grass is just a couch and the cedars a shady meeting place, not lessons about God's care. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/songs/1.htm
- One studylight commentary reads the "house" as the relationship the couple is building. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/song-of-solomon.html
- Gill: she praises the house he built for her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/songs/1.htm
